episode_title: The Last True Samurai: Hijikata Toshizo and the Shinsengumi's Final Stand
youtube_title: The Farmer's Son Who Died Defending a Country That Lasted 5 Months
youtube_description:
He was born a peasant with no right to carry a sword, and he ended up enforcing the samurai code more ruthlessly than anyone born into it. When the government he served collapsed, he cut his hair, put on a Western uniform, sailed to the far north, and was elected vice-minister of a republic that no other nation ever recognized. He died defending it, a week before it surrendered. This is the story of Hijikata Toshizo.

scenes.narration: Hijikata Toshizo was born in 1835 in Ishida, a farming village on the Tama plain west of Edo. He was the youngest of ten children, and his father died before he was born. The family made a homemade ointment for bruises and broken bones, and Toshizo carried it from village to village on his back — a peddler with a wooden box and a local reputation for winning fights. In his twenties he walked into a small country dojo teaching a rough sword style called Tennen Rishin-ryu. The man running it was a farmer's son too. His name was Kondo Isami.

scenes.narration: In the spring of 1863 the shogunate advertised for swordsmen. Kyoto had become ungovernable — imperial loyalists were murdering officials in the street and leaving the heads where they would be found — and the government wanted men willing to answer that in kind. Hijikata, Kondo and a handful of their students signed up, marched west with a corps of over two hundred, and arrived to find the whole scheme falling apart in political infighting. When the corps was ordered straight back to Edo, thirteen men refused to go. They stayed in Kyoto with no orders, no money, and no name.

scenes.narration: They found a patron in the Aizu domain, and by that autumn they had a name: Shinsengumi, the Newly Selected Corps. They also had a problem. Their nominal co-commander was a violent drunk who extorted merchants and burned down a shop over a refused loan, and he was destroying them faster than any enemy could. On a rainy night in the autumn of 1863, assassins walked into his lodging and killed him in his sleep. Almost every account points to Hijikata. From that night the corps had one commander, and one man to enforce his will.

scenes.narration: Hijikata wrote the corps regulations himself, and they were short and lethal. Do not deviate from the way of the warrior. Do not leave the corps. Do not fight private duels. The penalty attached to every clause was the same: seppuku. Over the next four years more Shinsengumi members died by their own hand under those rules than were ever killed by their enemies. Men began calling him the Demon Vice-Commander. He had understood something Kondo never did — that a unit of farmers and drifters playing at being samurai would only hold if leaving cost you your life.

scenes.narration: On a humid night in July 1864, the Shinsengumi raided an inn called the Ikedaya. Inside, loyalist radicals were finalizing a plan to set fire to Kyoto in a high wind and seize the emperor in the confusion. Kondo went through the door with only a handful of men and fought in the dark for close to two hours before Hijikata's larger detachment arrived and sealed the building. By morning the plot was dead. The Shinsengumi were suddenly the most feared police force in Japan — and the loyalists had learned a name they would never forgive.

scenes.narration: Success made the corps larger and harder to hold. In 1865 one of its own founding officers, the general manager, tried to leave. He was tracked down, brought back, and ordered to commit seppuku. Hijikata refused to make an exception for a man he had trained beside for years. Two years later a senior officer who had joined the corps preaching loyalty to the emperor broke away with a faction of his own. Hijikata had him cut down and left the body lying in the street as bait for the rest. They came for it. They died there.

scenes.narration: Then, in the summer of 1867, the impossible finally happened. The Shinsengumi were made direct retainers of the shogun. Hijikata Toshizo, the medicine peddler from Ishida village, was formally a samurai at last — the thing he had killed for and made other men kill themselves for. It lasted four months. That November the fifteenth shogun handed his authority back to the emperor, and the government the corps existed to protect simply stopped existing. The class Hijikata had just been admitted to was abolished from above, without a fight, by the man at the top of it.

scenes.narration: At the end of January 1868 the two sides met south of Kyoto, at Toba and Fushimi. The shogunate had roughly three times the men. It did not matter. The imperial forces had modern rifles and field artillery, and they broke the shogunal army in four days. The Shinsengumi charged with swords into rifle fire and were shattered as a fighting unit. Hijikata walked away from it with a conclusion most of his class refused to accept, and he said it out loud: swords and spears are of no further use. He never fought as a swordsman again.

scenes.narration: In April 1868 Kondo Isami surrendered at Nagareyama to buy time for his men. He was recognized, taken to Itabashi, and beheaded like a common criminal — no seppuku, no honor, his head sent to be displayed on the Kyoto riverbank where the corps had once hunted. Hijikata was not there. He was already fighting north at Utsunomiya, where a bullet went through his foot at the castle wall. When he could walk again, he had cut his topknot off, put on a Western military tunic and trousers, and stopped being a swordsman entirely. He was thirty-three.

scenes.narration: The war rolled north and took every ally he had with it — Utsunomiya, Bonari Pass, Aizu, Sendai. In October 1868 what was left of the shogunal forces boarded a fleet under Enomoto Takeaki and sailed for Ezo, the northern island now called Hokkaido. Hijikata took Matsumae castle in the snow at the head of a mixed infantry force. In December the officers held an election — the first ballot in Japanese history — and declared a republic based at the star-shaped fortress of Goryokaku. Hijikata Toshizo, born a peasant, was voted vice-minister of its army.

scenes.narration: The republic lasted five months. By May 1869 the imperial fleet had landed and Goryokaku was encircled. On the morning of the eleventh, hearing that his men holding the Benten battery down in the harbour were cut off and about to be overrun, Hijikata rode out toward them with a detachment of about fifty. At a roadblock called Ippongi a bullet struck him in the lower back. He is said to have stayed upright in the saddle for a moment before he went down. He was thirty-four years old. He died seven days before the surrender.

scenes.narration: He had known. Before the last fighting began he sent a young attendant out of the fortress carrying a package home to his family in Hino: a photograph taken in Hakodate, a lock of his hair, a letter, and his sword. The attendant got through. The photograph survives — a clean-shaven man in a dark Western uniform, seated, looking straight into the lens with an expression that gives absolutely nothing away. It is one of the clearest images we have of any samurai of that generation, and it exists because he arranged his own remembering before he rode out.

scenes.narration: Goryokaku surrendered on the eighteenth of May, 1869, and the Boshin War ended with it. Hijikata's body was buried somewhere in Hakodate by men who never recorded where; several temples claim him and none can prove it. Enomoto and most of the republic's leaders were pardoned within a few years and went on to serve the Meiji government — one of them ended up a cabinet minister. Hijikata was the only senior commander of that last army who did not live long enough to be forgiven.

scenes.narration: There is a manuscript held in Hino containing around forty haiku he wrote in his Kyoto years. They are, by general agreement, not very good — a swordsman's poems, blunt and literal, heavy on plum blossom and drawn blades. He gave the collection a title meaning something close to precious jewels, apparently without irony. His death poem is better. He wrote that though his body might rot on an island in the far north, his spirit would go east and stand guard over his lord. His lord had surrendered long before. He knew that when he wrote it.

scenes.narration: For most of a century after his death the Shinsengumi were the villains of the story — hired blades on the wrong side, thugs of a regime the country was glad to be rid of. What changed that was a novel. In 1964 the historical writer Shiba Ryotaro published a serialized life of Hijikata that recast him as the last man in Japan who actually believed in something. It has never gone out of print. Almost everything since — the films, the television dramas, the manga, the games — descends from that one book.

scenes.narration: Today the farmhouse in Hino where he was born is a small museum run by his family's descendants, and it still holds the sword he sent home. In Hakodate a bronze Hijikata stands near the ground where he was shot, and the star fort he died defending is now a public park with cherry trees planted along its ramparts. Every spring a few hundred people in pale blue haori march through Hino in his memory. Almost none of them are descended from samurai. Neither was he.

scenes.narration: That is the thing worth holding onto about Hijikata Toshizo. He was not defending a birthright, because he never had one. He was a peddler's son who chose a code that had never been offered to him, enforced it more literally than almost anyone born into it ever did, and then followed it past the point where the world it belonged to had ceased to exist. By the end he was not fighting for the shogun. He was fighting because he had decided who he was, and he would not be talked out of it.

scenes.narration: Next time on Samurai Chronicles: nine centuries before Hakodate, a warrior on the eastern plains conquered eight provinces, took the title of emperor for himself, and set up a rival court against Kyoto. He held it for two months. His severed head is said to have flown out of the capital and back east on its own — and the shrine built to calm it still stands in the middle of modern Tokyo. Taira no Masakado.
